claim_verdicts.evidence: RFC 9110 s4.3.5 defers IPv4 literals to "the 'IPv4address' ABNF rule ... see Section 3.2.2 of [URI]". RFC 3986 s3.2.2: "A host identified by an IPv4 literal address is represented in dotted-decimal notation (a sequence of four decimal numbers in the range 0 to 255, separated by '.')", with dec-octet capped at "25" %x30-35 = 255. The second half ("one machine can have more than one") is borne out by Docker engine networking, "Connecting to multiple networks", and by the box's own listing, which answers on 0.0.0.0 and on the IPv6 wildcard.

RFC 9293 s3.1 (TCP header format) gives Source Port "16 bits. The source port number." and Destination Port "16 bits. The destination port number." A 16-bit unsigned field takes exactly the values 0 through 65535, the range the lesson states. Fetched from rfc-editor.org; the wording above is what the page shows for the two fields.

RFC 1122 s3.2.1.3: "{ 127, <any> } Internal host loopback address. Addresses of this form MUST NOT appear outside a host." That is the lesson's "data never leaves" and it makes the block a per-host address; 127.0.0.1 lies inside it.

RFC 6761 s6.3: users "may assume that IPv4 and IPv6 address queries for localhost names will always resolve to the respective IP loopback address", and resolvers "SHOULD always return the IP loopback address for address queries" without querying external nameservers. Since the loopback address belongs to the host doing the lookup (claim 3), the name resolves to whichever machine runs the command. The section also covers ::1, which the lesson's four-number form leaves out but does not contradict.

RFC 1918 s3: "IANA has reserved the following three blocks of the IP address space for private internets: 10.0.0.0 - 10.255.255.255 (10/8 prefix), 172.16.0.0 - 172.31.255.255 (172.16/12 prefix), 192.168.0.0 - 192.168.255.255 (192.168/16 prefix)", and "routing information about private networks shall not be propagated on inter-enterprise links, and packets with private source or destination addresses should not be forwarded across such links." docker-compose.yml pins subnet 172.28.0.0/24, inside 172.16-172.31.

docker-compose.yml: service lab has networks.donhang.ipv4_address 172.28.0.12, service db has 172.28.0.11, networks.donhang.ipam.config subnet 172.28.0.0/24. Compose reference on ipv4_address: "Specify a static IP address for a service container when joining the network." Method note: git could not be run in this session, so files were read from the submodule working tree (branch auto/stage-0). The tag ref file was written 5 minutes after the branch tip, so it points at the tree I read; no code mismatch is being alleged.

Execution: outputs/stage-0/scripts/network/two-servers.txt shows the third listener refused ("nc: Address in use", exit code 1) while the SSH server holds 2222, and the first two get 9001/9002. Documented equivalent, PostgreSQL 17 s19.3.2: "could not bind IPv4 address 127.0.0.1: Address already in use / HINT: Is another postmaster already running on port 5432?", explained as "you tried to start another server on the same port where one is already running." The bind names an address as well as a number, which is the lesson's "on that same address".

Caddyfile at stage-0 has two site blocks served by one caddy:2.10.0 container: ":8080 { root * /srv/www ... }" and "donhang.local:8443 { tls internal ... }". The captured run shows both held at the same moment: "tcp 0 0 :::8080 :::* LISTEN" and "tcp 0 0 :::8443 :::* LISTEN". Condition not recorded in the ledger: that container is service web, not the lab box itself — see the section 4 issue.

The only allowed source that documents the case adds a condition the claim omits. PostgreSQL 17 s19.3.2, HINT: "Is another postmaster already running on port 5432? If not, wait a few seconds and retry." The "if not" branch is exactly the lesson's case — the holder is gone — and the documented advice is still to wait. Also tried: refs/ holds no POSIX or socket documentation, and neither captured output releases and re-claims a port, so the instant-availability reading has no execution evidence either.
claim_verdicts.suggested_text: The number is not owned, only held, and it can be claimed again once the process holding it is gone — though a program that asks in the very next instant may still be told the address is in use.

claim_verdicts.evidence: outputs/stage-0/scripts/network/who-listens.txt: "0.0.0.0:2222 ... LISTEN", ":::8080 ... LISTEN", ":::8443 ... LISTEN", and "localhost:9999 is closed". docker-compose.yml sets LISTEN_PORT "2222" on service lab (image built from lab/Dockerfile, lscr.io/linuxserver/openssh-server), and service web runs with network_mode "service:lab", so Caddy's two numbers show up in that box's listening list.

who-listens.sh:10 is `if nc -z -w 3 "$host" "$port" 2>/dev/null; then` — stderr discarded, only the exit status consumed, and the captured output carries nothing between the open/closed echoes, so the whole of its report is yes or no. Kubernetes docs use -z the same way: "You can use tools like netcat to check if a port is open. For example: nc 127.0.0.1 6443 -zv -w 2".

who-listens.sh:19 is `netstat -tln | grep -E ':(2222|8080|8443) ' | sort`, so 5432 could not have appeared in the listing — which is what the lesson now says, rather than resting on its absence. The other half stands on docker-compose.yml, where db is a separate service at 172.28.0.11 while the lab box is 172.28.0.12; the captured run reports "db:5432 is open".

ASP.NET Core 10 docs, section "Listen on all interfaces", lists `http://*:3000`, `http://+:3000` and `http://0.0.0.0:3000` as the samples that "demonstrate listening on all interfaces". Compose reference: "If you do not specify a host IP (such as 127.0.0.1), Docker binds to all interfaces (0.0.0.0)". The IPv4 qualifier matches the box's own listing, where 0.0.0.0:2222 and :::2222 are separate lines. Note the ledger's source_hint (RFC 1122 "{ 0, 0 } This host on this network") is about a datagram source address and does not settle this.

RFC 4291 s2.2: "The preferred form is x:x:x:x:x:x:x:x, where the 'x's are one to four hexadecimal digits of the eight 16-bit pieces of the address", and s2: "IPv6 addresses are 128-bit identifiers for interfaces and sets of interfaces" — a second family beside the four-number form, which is what the `:::2222` rows of the listing are.

outputs/stage-0/scripts/network/two-servers.txt matches the lesson's output block line for line once trailing spaces are normalised: "0.0.0.0:9001 ... LISTEN", "0.0.0.0:9002 ... LISTEN", then "nc: Address in use" and "   nc gave up with exit code 1". two-servers.sh lines 7-18 start nc on 9001 and 9002 in the background, sleep 1, print the netstat rows for 900[12], then run `nc -l 2222 || echo ...` reporting the exit code.

The two-wordings half is confirmed, the attribution half is not. PostgreSQL 17 prints "Address already in use" where the lab's nc prints "Address in use", so a second wording exists for the same refusal. But the same page calls that text the kernel's: "if the kernel error message is not Address already in use or some variant of that, there might be a different problem." The strings differ because the two boxes' error text differs, not only because each program picked its own words.
claim_verdicts.suggested_text: The wording differs from one program and one machine to the next, so another program refusing for the same reason may write `Address already in use` instead.

claim_verdicts.evidence: RFC 9293 s3.5.2: "If the connection does not exist (CLOSED), then a reset is sent in response to any incoming segment except another reset." A refusal is sent rather than silence, which is the lesson's "turns it away at once ... instead of leaving it unanswered", and it is why the captured run prints "localhost:9999 is closed" rather than the timeout `nc -z -w 3` was prepared to wait for. The three-second timing itself was not measured; only the reported result is in the transcript.

docker-compose.yml: db is its own service (postgres:17.6-alpine, hostname db) at 172.28.0.11; the only service sharing the lab box's network is web (network_mode "service:lab"), which is caddy:2.10.0. lab/Dockerfile installs postgresql17-client only — a client, no server — so nothing in that box's network listens on 5432, and db's "ports: 5432:5432" publishes to the host machine, not into the box. Docker docs: "The Docker container uses its own network namespace, and resolves loopback addresses such as 127.0.0.1 to itself."

Compose networking: "Each service registers its name with an internal DNS server, so containers can reach each other using the service name directly. No IP addresses or manual configuration is needed." In this repo the service is named db, carries hostname db, and joins network donhang with ipv4_address 172.28.0.11, so inside the lab network the name stands for that address — and the captured run reports "db:5432 is open" from the lab box.
